title: Highest-Protein Cheeses: Ranking per 100 Grams and Serving

seo.title: Highest-Protein Cheeses: Ranking
seo.meta_description: Compare Parmesan, Romano, Gruyère, Swiss, cheddar and mozzarella by protein per 100 grams and realistic serving size.
seo.search_intent: Compare cheeses by protein and understand the effect of moisture and aging.

excerpt: Parmesan, Romano and Gruyère are among the highest-protein cheeses per 100 g because they contain relatively little water. Fresh cheeses are less concentrated but can provide more total protein in a larger serving.
content_html:
Hard aged cheeses are protein-dense because pressing and aging remove water. The same process concentrates fat, calcium and sodium, so protein concentration is only one part of the nutritional picture.

Protein per 100 g

CheeseApprox. protein
Parmesan35.8 g
Pecorino Romano~31.9 g
Gruyère~29.8 g
Swiss/Emmental style~27 g
Provolone~25.6 g
Cheddar~25 g
Gouda~25 g
Low-moisture mozzarella~24 g
Feta~14 g
Cottage cheese~11–13 g

Parmesan

Parmesan provides about 35.8 g protein/100 g. A 1-ounce / 28 g serving supplies about 10 g protein. It is highly concentrated, but that small serving also brings roughly 110 calories and substantial sodium.

Romano and Gruyère

Romano is around 32 g/100 g and Gruyère near 30 g. A 1-ounce serving provides roughly 8–9 g protein.

Cheddar, Gouda and Provolone

These cluster around 25–26 g/100 g. One ounce provides about 7 g protein, close to the 6–7 g in a large egg.

Mozzarella

Low-moisture mozzarella can reach about 24 g/100 g, while fresh mozzarella contains much more water and may be closer to 18–20 g. The moisture difference explains much of the gap.

Fresh cheeses

Cottage cheese is often around 11–13 g/100 g, about one-third of Parmesan by weight. But a 1-cup / ~200 g bowl can provide 22–26 g protein, more total protein than a normal Parmesan serving.

Why aging concentrates protein

As water leaves the cheese, more milk solids remain in each 100 g. Aging does not create new protein; it increases the concentration by weight.

Protein by serving

CheeseServingProtein
Parmesan1 oz / 28 g10 g
Gruyère1 oz / 28 g8–9 g
Cheddar1 oz / 28 g7 g
Low-moisture mozzarella2 oz / 56 g13 g
Cottage cheese1 cup / ~200 g22–26 g

Calcium, fat and sodium

Hard cheeses can be excellent calcium sources, but they also concentrate saturated fat and sodium. Low-fat cottage cheese may provide less protein per 100 g while supplying far fewer calories per that weight.

Bottom line

Parmesan, Romano and Gruyère lead by concentration. For a larger serving with lower calorie density, high-protein fresh cheeses can provide more total protein. Moisture, fat, sodium and serving size matter as much as the ranking position.

Sources

Composition values come from USDA FoodData Central. Commercial cheese labels remain useful because moisture and formulation vary by brand.

faq.question: Which cheese has the most protein?
faq.answer: Parmesan is among the most concentrated at about 35.8 g/100 g, followed by Romano near 32 g and Gruyère near 30 g.

faq.question: Why does aged cheese have more protein?
faq.answer: It contains less water, so protein and other milk solids are more concentrated by weight.

faq.question: Is cottage cheese low in protein?
faq.answer: It is less concentrated, around 11–13 g/100 g, but a full cup can provide more than 20 g protein.
